title: Glossary — Plain-Language Definitions
subtitle: Every term used in this manual and in the program, explained in one or two plain sentences. Radio jargon, propagation words, and the program's own labels are all here.

callout.label: HOW TO USE THIS
callout.text: Hit a word you don't know? Find it here. Terms are grouped by topic and defined in everyday language — no prior knowledge assumed. Each definition points you to the chapter where the term is used in depth.

rows: A licensed hobby of two-way radio communication for personal, experimental, and emergency use.
A range of frequencies set aside for amateur use, named by wavelength — e.g. "20 meters," "40 meters."
Continuous Wave — Morse code. A very efficient mode that gets through when voice can't.
Voice modes, most commonly SSB (Single Sideband). "Phone" just means talking, as opposed to Morse or digital.
Sending data (like FT8) rather than voice or Morse; the computer does the sending and decoding.
Operating at low power — 5 to 10 watts. Popular for lightweight, battery-friendly field operating.
A two-way contact/conversation between two stations.
A frequency where operators of a given mode gather to find each other.
Your level of amateur license (Technician, General, or Amateur Extra), which sets what frequencies and modes you may use.
The share of your on-air time actually spent transmitting versus listening — matters for battery life.
How radio signals travel from one place to another — which bands reach where, and when.
A high layer of the atmosphere that bends shortwave signals back to Earth, letting them skip long distances.
The program's headline score for a band: roughly, the chance a contact will succeed. Higher and greener is better. (Chapter 4)
The single time of day a band is predicted to be at its best, shown in UTC. (Chapter 4)
Maximum Usable Frequency — the highest frequency the ionosphere is bending back on your path right now. Bands below it tend to work; above it usually don't. (Chapter 4)
A count of sunspots, used as a simple measure of solar activity. Higher generally means better high-band conditions. (Chapter 4)
The sun's radio energy at 10.7 cm; moves with the sunspot number and tells the same story. Higher favors the high bands. (Chapter 4)
A near-real-time 0–9 gauge of how disturbed Earth's magnetic field is. Low is calm and good; 5+ is a geomagnetic storm that degrades the bands. (Chapter 4)
A once-a-day summary of geomagnetic disturbance, companion to the K-index. Low is good. (Chapter 4)
The twilight band circling the Earth at sunrise/sunset, when low bands can reach unusually far. (Chapter 8)
Near Vertical Incidence Skywave — sending signals nearly straight up so they rain back down over a nearby region; used for regional/emergency coverage. (Chapters 4, 6)
Reaching a station the long way around the globe instead of the direct route. (Chapter 4)
Coordinated Universal Time — the single worldwide time zone radio operators share. (Chapter 15)
A map of an antenna's "loudness" in every direction. (Chapter 7)
The angle above the horizon where an antenna radiates most strongly. Low = long distance; high = nearby/regional. (Chapter 7)
How much an antenna concentrates the signal in its best direction, versus a reference antenna. Measured in dBi. (Chapter 7)
For a directional antenna, how much stronger it is forward than backward. (Chapter 7)
The top-down view of a pattern — which compass directions the signal favors. (Chapter 7)
The side-on view of a pattern — at what angle above the horizon the signal leaves. (Chapter 7)
A basic antenna: a wire fed in the center. Its height sets its take-off angle. (Chapter 3)
An antenna that stands upright, often with radials; radiates low and all around — good for distance. (Chapter 3)
An end-fed wire antenna (End-Fed Half-Wave and similar), fed at one end rather than the middle. (Chapter 3)
Wires laid at the base of a vertical that act as its electrical "ground." How many and how long affects performance. (Chapter 3)
Where the coax cable connects to the antenna (center, end, off-center, or base). A required detail for modeling. (Chapter 3)
A flag on each antenna's pattern: Measured = trust it; Approximate = a good guide for loaded/broadband antennas a simple model can't capture exactly. (Chapter 7)
The physical length of one radio wave; antenna dimensions are often described as fractions of it (e.g. quarter-wave).
The propagation-prediction engine the program runs behind the scenes to rank bands. (Chapters 2, 4)
The antenna-modeling engine the program runs to compute radiation patterns. (Chapters 2, 7)
The one-time, step-by-step screen that collects your gear the first time you run the program. (Chapter 2)
Your saved list of owned gear, editable any time. (Chapter 3)
The kind of operation you're planning (POTA, SOTA, Field Day, EMCOMM, General), which tailors gear and framing. (Chapter 6)
The fast path that gives full recommendations with no setup. (Chapter 5)
The program keeps no session history; each plan uses the current time and conditions. (Chapters 4, 9)
A short code (like EM29) naming your location on the map; the program converts it to/from latitude and longitude. (Chapter 14)
Guessing your location from your internet connection — convenient but only rough, and often wrong on a hotspot. (Chapter 14)
A device (often USB) that reports your exact position from satellites; the most accurate location source. (Chapter 14)
Portable Document Format — the file type the program exports plans and checklists to for printing or carrying. (Chapters 4, 6)
A measure of battery capacity — roughly, amps × hours it can supply. (Chapter 12)
The program's color scheme, switchable between Auto, Light, and Dark. (Chapter 15)
